narrative.title: How do you just make things happen?
narrative.body:
People have asked me my whole life how I just make things happen. I never had a good answer until recently.

As a Spanish speaking volunteer across three states, I inherited a territory the group before me had written off. I built it into our most productive account through one relationship that unlocked everything. A corporate career took me from Vivint, where I identified a $2M opportunity and sold it to senior leadership, to Goldman Sachs, where my hiring manager called my interview one of the best he had ever seen. Most recently, finishing my EMT program in the top 5% of my class, I found myself in emergency rooms and trauma bays executing under pressure alongside physicians and their teams.

Different rooms. Same instinct. Read the person. Understand what they need. Earn their trust. Find a way to close the gap.

That is what a physician's office manager, a specialist, and a nurse all need from the person walking through their door representing a product. I know how to cover a territory, build relationships with everyone in the office from the physician to the front desk, learn dense clinical material fast, and stay compliant while doing it. I already drive my own territory well, and I am looking for a patient-focused, innovation-driven company to bring that to, one that puts quality, integrity, and partnership first.

startStories.title: The Territory Everyone Wrote Off
startStories.teaser: I was assigned a territory where the key stakeholder had already said no before I ever showed up, and the numbers proved it.
startStories.body:
My job was to find people willing to join our group. Cold calling strangers rarely worked. Warm introductions did. In each area, one key local contact connected us to the people we needed to reach. Mine had shut out everyone before me, and the territory's numbers showed it.

I did not push. I got to know his wife first, no agenda, just showing up over time. Eventually she mentioned he missed playing soccer. That was my opening. We organized a game, he came, and we kept it going. He went from closed off to actively introducing us to his whole network.

A no is not the end. It just means you have not found the right way in yet, and that trust cannot be rushed. That is exactly what it takes with a physician who has already turned away every rep before you.

startStories.title: The Goldman Standard
startStories.teaser: At Goldman I managed multi million dollar loan portfolios where one missed detail buried in a hundred page contract meant real money and real trust on the line.
startStories.body:
I managed a portfolio of institutional clients across multi million dollar loan accounts. The contracts behind those deals ran hundreds of pages of dense language, and a single detail buried at one point could not be missed. I learned to read them front to back so I caught discrepancies before they ever reached a client.

When clients had questions I answered in plain terms, not legal speak, because their trust in me depended on actually understanding what I told them. I kept every deadline I gave, including working from a plane on Christmas Eve once, because the commitment mattered more than the inconvenience.

Accuracy and warmth are not a tradeoff. A physician's office expects the same thing from a rep: someone who is never wrong on the details and values their time as much as their own.

startStories.title: The Rooftop Trauma Night
startStories.teaser: Three months into my EMT program, an emergency air transport put me in a trauma bay with a team I had never worked with before, and no time to think about it.
startStories.body:
I was three months into my EMT program, about 2am during a 12 hour overnight shift. My mentor pulled me mid task and told me to follow two nurses immediately. We ran to the rooftop helipad to receive an emergency air transport, learning the protocol on the way up, then raced the patient into the trauma bay.

The surgeon barked a command to cut the patient's clothes off. I stepped forward and started cutting while he performed what I later identified as an emergency tracheotomy. A couple of other students in the room had frozen. The nurses told them to follow my lead.

You do not rise to the occasion, you fall to your level of preparation. A team that trusts its training moves together without anyone having to think twice, whether that is a trauma bay or a physician's office.
